newsitem.title: BULGARIA: After euphoria, tough times lie ahead for Bulgaria.
newsitem.headline: After euphoria, tough times lie ahead for Bulgaria.

text.p: As the euphoria of victory over their ex-communist rulers wears off, Bulgarians must return to the daily reality of living in Europe's most crisis-ridden economy, with its bread and petrol queues and soaring prices.

After 30 days of mass street protests, the Bulgarian Socialist Party on Tuesday agreed to give up attempts to form another government and President Petar Stoyanov brokered a deal for general elections in April.

Opposition supporters celebrated late into the night but by Wednesday morning people were back in their bread queues, and political victory will do nothing to resolve petrol shortages looming from a cash crisis at Bulgaria's biggest oil refinery.

"We must celebrate now because we have very hard days ahead," Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), told supporters on Tuesday after the agreement was announced.
The UDF and Socialists will both have to settle internal differences and design election campaigns which woo voters but raise no false hopes about their grim economic future.
"They need to be very realistic now and prepare people for future problems," said one Sofia-based diplomat.
"Things aren't going to get better and they're likely to get worse in the run-up to elections."

Though the Socialist government has lost all credibility -- one poll last month put their support at eight percent -- protesters were on the streets primarily because of economic hardship rather than support for the opposition.
Outgoing Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21 after months of criticism of his handling of the economy.
Since then nothing has been done to stem the crisis and the lev currency is in free fall. Inflation for January alone is put at 50 percent, and for 1997 it is forecast in four figures.

"Civil protests in the country will stop and people will return to their homes but the workers who went on strike also have many economic and social demands," Konstantin Trenchev, leader of the Podkrepa trade union, told Troud daily.
"In many places they are calling not only for higher salaries in line with inflation, but also for a change of their incompetent managers."
Most miners went back to work on Wednesday but two mines are still on strike for more pay.
Once work resumes on rescuing the remains of the economy, reforms will include closure of loss-making state enterprises, putting thousands out of work.

For now, the signs are that the electorate is prepared for more austerity, provided it can trust its leaders. When Stoyanov warned cheering crowds at the presidency on Tuesday of hard times to come, they chanted back: "We are with you".
"I do not promise you that you will be richer or you will live better, I promise you that under the next government I will be honest and you will be master of your lives," Stoyanov told the crowd.
Bulgaria's communists renamed themselves Socialists after the collapse of one-party rule in 1989 and have governed almost without interruption since then.
The UDF had a short-lived government under Filip Dimitrov from November 1991 to December 1992, which is principally remembered for its disastrous attempts at land reform.

Both the Socialists and the UDF are deeply divided, and the prospect of elections is likely to revive an arcane internal debate in the opposition coalition over whether it should become a single party.

The Socialists were elected in December 1994 for a four-year term, but, with poverty and crime worsening, the electorate turned against them last November and elected Stoyanov on the ticket of the united opposition.
If the UDF can keep up the momentum of the past month and win the elections, their prime minister would be Kostov, a 47-year-old economist who was finance minister under Dimitrov.

Local media cite Sofia's respected UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski as one possible candidate to head a caretaker cabinet, which Stoyanov must appoint by February 20, dissolving parliament at the same time.
The International Monetary Fund offered one sign of hope on Wednesday, saying it would resume talks on a new programme as soon as an interim government was in place.
